analysis.one_liner: Bans insured banks from making or financing payday loans and outlaws payday loans repaid through insured accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and no vote, leaving payday loans averaging 390% to 780% APR in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for a bank with federal deposit insurance to make or finance a payday loan, and illegal for any lender to issue a payday loan repaid through a check or debit on an account at an insured bank or credit union — how nearly all payday loans get repaid. It also would have directed the Federal Reserve to study requiring clear APR advertising and a high-interest warning label on any loan above 36% APR. The bill's findings cited average rates of 390% to 780% APR and typical customers taking 8 to 12 loans a year.
analysis.who_benefits: People who take payday loans — the bill's findings describe them as individuals with limited access to affordable credit facing immediate needs — would keep more of their money instead of paying fees that compound into 390% to 780% APR. States could enforce their interest-rate caps again, since lenders could no longer route loans through a partner bank to claim federal preemption. Borrowers would also gain the right to sue violating lenders for damages and legal fees.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions from making any payday loan directly or indirectly, and from lending money to other lenders to finance, refinance, or extend payday loans.

Bars any creditor from making a payday loan repaid by a personal check or debit authorization on an account at an insured bank or credit union — the collection method for virtually all payday loans — and gives borrowers the right to sue violating lenders for damages and legal fees.

Would restore states' ability to enforce their interest-rate caps, since the bill's findings state that lenders had affiliated with insured banks to use federal preemption to 'circumvent interest rate regulation in State law.'
Directs the Federal Reserve to study and recommend the most effective way to require finance-charge and APR advertising plus a high-interest warning label on any loan above 36% APR.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders would lose the product entirely, and the banks that earned fees originating or financing payday loans would lose that business. Borrowers with an urgent cash need and no access to bank credit would have one fewer option, and the bill offers no substitute, so some would turn to overdrafts, late fees, or informal lenders.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans the payday loan without creating or funding any affordable small-dollar alternative, so borrowers facing an emergency cash shortfall could be left with overdraft fees, late fees, or informal and illegal lenders.

The Truth in Lending Act prohibition applies only when a creditor 'knows or has reasonable cause to believe' the loan is collected from an insured account, leaving room for lenders to dispute liability case by case.
Enforcement would rest mainly on borrowers bringing private lawsuits for damages and legal fees, a slow remedy for someone in an immediate cash crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers caught in repeat cycles, eliminating a product that the bill's own findings say runs 390% to 780% APR and typically 8 to 12 loans a year outweighs the loss of access, and restoring state rate caps is a real gain. But the bill is one-sided in design: it removes the product without building an alternative, and a borrower with a car repair and no cash would face the same emergency with fewer options, since overdrafts, late fees, and informal lenders carry their own heavy costs. The TILA "knows or has reasonable cause to believe" standard also leaves room for lenders to argue they did not know the account was insured. A stronger bill would have paired the ban with an affordable small-dollar channel; this one does not.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2006 with no cosponsors, it was referred to the Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Tom Udall introduced the bill on May 10, 2006 and delivered introductory remarks the same day (CR E788).
No member of either party cosponsored the bill.

The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services on May 10, 2006, and on May 22, 2006 to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit; no further action appears in the record.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill's own findings put average payday loan rates at 390% to 780% APR for a two-week loan, with a typical customer taking 8 to 12 loans a year at a single lender.

The findings state that payday lenders affiliated with insured depository institutions to invoke the federal 'most favored lender' principle and circumvent state interest-rate regulation — the loophole the bill was written to close.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders kept their business, including the bank-partnership route around state rate caps, and their partner banks kept the fee income; borrowers kept facing loans averaging 390% to 780% APR.

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 10, 2006 and delivered introductory remarks (CR E788); he was its only sponsor, with no cosponsors.

against.name: Michael G. Oxley
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never held a hearing or markup; the bill sat at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew one Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors from either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill defines 'payday loan' structurally and bans collecting one by check or debit from any insured bank or credit union account, which covers essentially the whole product; the bill's findings note customers typically take 8 to 12 loans a year at a single lender, which is where lender revenue comes from. It also closes the bank-partnership route lenders used to claim federal preemption from state rate caps.

Banks could no longer make, finance, or extend payday loans, ending fee income from the partnerships the bill's findings say existed to circumvent state interest-rate regulation. Most banks never made payday loans, so the direct hit fell on the partner-bank niche.

The ban on collecting payday loans from credit union accounts applies to credit unions too, but only to payday-structured loans; member-owned credit unions generally charge far less than payday lenders, so their cheaper small-dollar lending would continue.
